subtopic_detail: responding to escalating prescribed opioid use for chronic non cancer pain with declining function
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 47 year old man who has taken sustained release oxycodone for chronic low back pain for five years. He has inherited this prescription from a previous doctor and asks you today for an increase.

He is now on 80 mg of oral morphine equivalent daily, having started on 20 mg. He tells you the pain is no better than when he started and that he has stopped playing golf and has been off work for two years. He says he gets a few hours of relief after each dose and is watching the clock towards the end of the interval. He has run out early twice in the past four months. He drinks no alcohol and uses no illicit drugs, and a urine drug screen shows only his prescribed medication. He has not had a trial of any non pharmacological pain programme. His imaging shows degenerative change only.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 74/min, blood pressure 128/80 mmHg, respiratory rate 15/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 36.5 degrees C
data_table.Examination: No focal neurological deficit in either leg, straight leg raise negative bilaterally, reflexes symmetrical, no saddle anaesthesia, no bladder or bowel disturbance, guarded lumbar movement
data_table.Investigations: Urine drug screen positive for the prescribed opioid only, lumbar magnetic resonance imaging shows degenerative disc disease with no nerve root compression, liver and renal function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Increase the dose as requested and review his pain scores in four weeks
options.rationale: Dose escalation would be considered where a clear analgesic benefit had been demonstrated and function was improving, which is the opposite of his trajectory over five years. Escalating in the face of declining function and no analgesic gain increases harm without any prospect of benefit. (Source: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Prescribing drugs of dependence)
source_refs: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Prescribing drugs of dependence

options.text: Cease the opioid abruptly today and manage any withdrawal symptomatically
options.rationale: Abrupt cessation after five years of continuous use produces severe withdrawal and commonly drives patients to illicit sources or to other prescribers, which is more dangerous than continued prescribing. Rapid discontinuation in this population is associated with increased overdose and suicide risk. (Source: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Prescribing drugs of dependence)
source_refs: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Prescribing drugs of dependence

options.text: Negotiate a structured tapering plan with a broader pain management approach
options.rationale: Chronic non cancer pain that has not improved over five years while function has steadily declined indicates that the opioid is not delivering analgesia, and slow tapering at around ten percent of the dose every two to four weeks typically maintains or improves both pain and function. The taper must be paired with active substitutes, meaning a multidisciplinary pain programme, graded exercise and psychological therapy, because withdrawing the drug without offering anything in its place is what makes these conversations fail. (Source: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Prescribing drugs of dependence)
source_refs: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Prescribing drugs of dependence

options.text: Add a benzodiazepine to help with the muscle spasm and his difficulty sleeping
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines combined with opioids markedly increase the risk of respiratory depression and death, and this combination features in a large proportion of opioid related fatalities. They also have no role in chronic low back pain beyond a few days. (Source: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Prescribing drugs of dependence)
source_refs: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Prescribing drugs of dependence

options.text: Discharge him from the practice and advise him to find another prescriber
options.rationale: Abandonment leaves a dependent patient without care and simply transfers the problem, and it is the response most likely to result in harm. The clinical situation calls for active management of a treatment that is no longer working rather than disengagement. (Source: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Prescribing drugs of dependence)
source_refs: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Prescribing drugs of dependence

explanation.summary: Long term opioid therapy for chronic non cancer pain has weak evidence of sustained analgesic benefit and clear evidence of harm including tolerance, dependence, hyperalgesia, endocrine suppression and overdose. The markers that this treatment has failed are present here: no reduction in pain over five years, progressive loss of function, clock watching before doses and early prescription exhaustion. Tolerance and opioid induced hyperalgesia both mean that escalating the dose will not restore benefit. The appropriate response is a negotiated, gradual taper, commonly around ten percent of the dose every two to four weeks with slower steps at lower doses, undertaken alongside a multidisciplinary pain approach combining graded activity, psychological therapy and non opioid analgesia. Abrupt cessation and discharge from care both increase the risk of overdose and should be avoided.
key_points: Long term opioids for chronic non cancer pain show weak analgesic benefit with substantial harms.
Loss of function, clock watching and running out early indicate the treatment is failing.
Opioid induced hyperalgesia means dose escalation may worsen rather than relieve pain.
Taper gradually, around ten percent every two to four weeks, with slower steps at lower doses.
Combining opioids with benzodiazepines markedly increases the risk of fatal respiratory depression.
explanation.pearls: Measure function rather than pain scores when reviewing long term opioid therapy, because a patient who has stopped working and stopped exercising while his pain is unchanged has already demonstrated that the drug is not working, and that is the argument for a taper rather than an increase.

sources.label: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Prescribing drugs of dependence
Faculty of Pain Medicine, Australian and New Zealand College of Anaesthetists

subtopic_detail: responding to a markedly prolonged corrected QT interval in an older patient whose antidepressant dose exceeds the age adjusted maximum
stem:
You are the consultation liaison psychiatry registrar asked to review a 71 year old woman admitted with a fractured wrist after a fall at home. She has taken citalopram 40 mg daily for two years for recurrent major depression and her mood has been stable.

The orthopaedic team have sent an electrocardiogram because she described two episodes of feeling faint in the week before the fall. She takes no other regular medication apart from a thiazide diuretic for hypertension and a proton pump inhibitor. She has had no chest pain and no palpitations. Her potassium is 3.1 mmol/L and her magnesium is 0.62 mmol/L. Her electrocardiogram shows sinus rhythm at 64 beats per minute with a corrected QT interval of 512 ms, and a tracing from three years ago showed a corrected QT interval of 430 ms.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 64/min, blood pressure 138/82 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 36.5 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Alert and oriented, mood euthymic with reactive affect, no psychotic features, no tremor or clonus, heart sounds dual with no murmur, chest clear
data_table.Investigations: Corrected QT interval 512 ms against 430 ms three years ago, potassium 3.1 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), magnesium 0.62 mmol/L (0.70-1.10), corrected calcium 2.30 mmol/L (2.10-2.60), thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Continue citalopram at 40 mg and repeat the electrocardiogram in three months
options.rationale: Continuing unchanged would be defensible if the interval were mildly prolonged and stable with no symptoms, and a corrected QT of 512 ms with presyncope sits in the range where torsades de pointes becomes a real risk. Her dose also exceeds the maximum recommended above 65 years, so the exposure driving the prolongation is itself inappropriate. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Switch to amitriptyline at a low dose, which also treats her neuropathic pain
options.rationale: Tricyclic antidepressants block cardiac sodium and potassium channels and prolong the QT interval more than most selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, so this would worsen the specific problem. They also carry anticholinergic and orthostatic effects that increase falls risk in an older woman who has just fallen. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Stop all antidepressant treatment permanently and monitor her mood in clinic
options.rationale: Complete withdrawal would expose a woman with recurrent major depression to a high risk of relapse, and the problem is drug and dose specific rather than a contraindication to the whole class. Effective alternatives with minimal effect on the QT interval exist. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Halve the citalopram to 20 mg and take no other action on the abnormal results
options.rationale: Reducing to 20 mg does bring the dose to the maximum recommended above 65 years and is a necessary part of the answer, but it leaves the hypokalaemia and hypomagnesaemia untreated. Those electrolyte abnormalities are independently arrhythmogenic and are contributing substantially to an interval of 512 ms. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Correct the electrolytes, cease citalopram and change to a safer antidepressant
options.rationale: A corrected QT interval above 500 ms with presyncope requires the offending drug to be withdrawn rather than reduced, and citalopram at 40 mg exceeds the 20 mg maximum recommended above 65 years because prolongation is dose dependent. Replacing potassium and magnesium is equally important since both deficits independently prolong repolarisation, and sertraline or mirtazapine can then continue her treatment with minimal effect on the interval. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

explanation.summary: Citalopram and its enantiomer escitalopram prolong the QT interval in a dose dependent way, which is why the maximum recommended citalopram dose falls to 20 mg daily above 65 years and in hepatic impairment or with interacting drugs. This woman has been taking twice that maximum. Her thiazide has produced hypokalaemia and hypomagnesaemia, and both independently prolong repolarisation, so the abnormal interval has several correctable contributors acting together. A corrected QT above 500 ms with presyncope is the threshold at which the culprit drug is ceased rather than merely reduced. Sertraline and mirtazapine have minimal effect on the interval and are appropriate substitutes, while tricyclics would make matters worse.
key_points: Citalopram prolongs the QT interval dose dependently, with a maximum of 20 mg daily above 65 years.
Hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia and hypocalcaemia each independently prolong the QT interval.
A corrected QT above 500 ms or a rise of more than 60 ms from baseline is the threshold for ceasing the culprit drug.
Tricyclic antidepressants prolong the QT interval more than most selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors.
Sertraline and mirtazapine have minimal effect on cardiac repolarisation and are suitable alternatives.
explanation.pearls: Check the citalopram dose against age whenever you see a prolonged QT interval, because 40 mg is twice the recommended maximum above 65 years, and always replace potassium and magnesium at the same time since a thiazide induced deficit commonly contributes more to the interval than the antidepressant does.

subtopic_detail: recognising sudden loss of muscle tone triggered by laughter in a young man referred with suspected depression
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 19 year old university student referred by his mother because he sleeps all the time and she is worried he is depressed.

He describes falling asleep in lectures and once while sitting on a bus, and says brief naps leave him refreshed for an hour or two. He is not sad, is looking forward to the summer, has been going out with friends and has not lost interest in his hobbies. His appetite and weight are unchanged and he denies any thoughts of self harm. He mentions that when his friends make him laugh hard his knees buckle and his jaw goes slack for a few seconds while he stays fully aware, and that he sometimes wakes unable to move for half a minute and sees a figure in the doorway that is not there.

data_table.Examination: Normal neurological examination, normal power and reflexes, no ptosis, no fatigable weakness, body mass index 24 kg/m2, mood euthymic with reactive affect
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, iron studies, thyroid function and fasting glucose all within normal limits, Epworth Sleepiness Scale score 19 out of 24

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Major depressive disorder presenting with hypersomnia and low motivation
options.rationale: Atypical depression does feature hypersomnia and leaden heaviness of the limbs, and it requires low mood or loss of interest, both of which are absent in a young man who is socialising, enjoying his hobbies and looking forward to the summer. Depressive hypersomnia also leaves patients unrefreshed rather than restored by a short nap. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines)

options.text: Narcolepsy with cataplexy caused by loss of hypocretin signalling
options.rationale: Sudden bilateral loss of muscle tone triggered by strong emotion with fully preserved awareness is cataplexy, which is close to specific for this condition and reflects intrusion of the muscle atonia of rapid eye movement sleep into wakefulness. Sleep paralysis and hypnagogic hallucinations are further manifestations of the same intrusion, and refreshing short naps distinguish this from the unrefreshing sleep of depression or sleep apnoea. (Source: Sleep Health Foundation: Narcolepsy)

options.text: Obstructive sleep apnoea producing fragmented sleep and daytime somnolence
options.rationale: Sleep apnoea is an important cause of daytime sleepiness and characteristically occurs with obesity, snoring and witnessed apnoeas, none of which is described in a young man with a body mass index of 24 kg/m2. It also does not produce emotion triggered loss of tone or refreshing naps. (Source: Sleep Health Foundation: Narcolepsy)

options.text: Focal epilepsy with atonic seizures and associated postictal confusion
options.rationale: Atonic seizures cause abrupt loss of tone and would be a reasonable consideration, but they impair awareness and are followed by confusion, whereas he remains fully alert throughout and recovers instantly. Reliable triggering by laughter rather than by anything else also fits emotional rather than epileptic physiology. (Source: Sleep Health Foundation: Narcolepsy)

options.text: Delayed sleep phase disorder with chronic insufficient sleep on weeknights
options.rationale: Circadian phase delay is very common in this age group and produces sleepiness through simple sleep restriction, with normal sleep quality and duration when the person is allowed to choose their own hours. It offers no explanation for cataplexy, sleep paralysis or hallucinations at sleep onset. (Source: Sleep Health Foundation: Narcolepsy)

explanation.summary: Narcolepsy typically begins in adolescence or early adulthood and is frequently misattributed to depression, laziness or poor sleep habits for years before diagnosis. The tetrad is excessive daytime sleepiness, cataplexy, sleep paralysis and hypnagogic or hypnopompic hallucinations, and the last three all represent intrusion of rapid eye movement sleep phenomena into wakefulness. Cataplexy, meaning sudden bilateral loss of muscle tone triggered by strong emotion with fully preserved consciousness, is the feature that makes the diagnosis and separates it from atonic seizures and syncope. The mechanism in narcolepsy with cataplexy is loss of hypocretin producing neurons in the lateral hypothalamus, probably autoimmune. Diagnosis is confirmed by polysomnography followed by a multiple sleep latency test.
key_points: Cataplexy is bilateral loss of tone triggered by emotion with fully preserved awareness and no postictal phase.
Short naps are refreshing in narcolepsy and unrefreshing in depression and obstructive sleep apnoea.
Sleep paralysis and hypnagogic hallucinations reflect intrusion of rapid eye movement phenomena into wakefulness.
Loss of hypothalamic hypocretin neurons underlies narcolepsy with cataplexy.
Diagnosis requires overnight polysomnography followed by a multiple sleep latency test the next day.
explanation.pearls: Ask directly whether anything happens to the muscles when the patient laughs, because cataplexy is close to diagnostic of narcolepsy and patients rarely volunteer it, having usually interpreted their buckling knees as clumsiness rather than as a neurological symptom.

subtopic_detail: balancing the risk of refeeding against the risk of continued underfeeding in a severely malnourished adolescent
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar admitting a 15 year old girl with anorexia nervosa who has lost 16 kg over eight months. She is on day two of admission to a specialist adolescent unit with continuous cardiac monitoring.

She was started on a nutrition plan yesterday and her intake is being supervised. Overnight her heart rate fell to 38 beats per minute while asleep and she has had one episode of dizziness on standing. Her weight for height is 68 percent of expected. She has no oedema and no confusion. Her phosphate was 1.10 mmol/L on admission and is 0.72 mmol/L this morning, her magnesium has fallen from 0.88 to 0.71 mmol/L, and her potassium has fallen from 3.9 to 3.4 mmol/L. Her electrocardiogram shows sinus bradycardia with a corrected QT interval of 440 ms and no arrhythmia. The dietitian asks whether the energy intake should be held or reduced.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 38/min asleep and 46/min awake, blood pressure 88/52 mmHg lying and 74/46 mmHg standing, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 35.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Emaciated with lanugo hair, cool peripheries with capillary refill 3 seconds, no peripheral or sacral oedema, no crackles, Glasgow coma scale 15, no confusion or weakness
data_table.Investigations: Phosphate fallen from 1.10 to 0.72 mmol/L (0.80-1.50), magnesium fallen from 0.88 to 0.71 mmol/L (0.70-1.10), potassium fallen from 3.9 to 3.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), corrected QT interval 440 ms, glucose 3.6 mmol/L (3.0-5.4), thiamine given on admission

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of her nutrition?

options.text: Halve the energy intake until the electrolytes return to the normal range
options.rationale: Reducing intake in response to falling electrolytes is the traditional cautious approach and is now recognised to cause harm, because prolonged underfeeding produces its own syndrome of continued weight loss, worsening bradycardia and delayed recovery. The falling electrolytes are a predictable and treatable consequence of feeding rather than a signal to stop. (Source: RCH CPG: Eating disorders)

options.text: Cease enteral intake entirely and commence parenteral nutrition instead
options.rationale: Parenteral nutrition carries line sepsis and thrombosis risks and does not avoid refeeding syndrome, which is driven by the metabolic shift from catabolism to carbohydrate use regardless of the route. The gut is working and should be used. (Source: RCH CPG: Eating disorders)

options.text: Continue the current intake unchanged and recheck the electrolytes in 48 hours
options.rationale: Continuing to feed is correct, and a 48 hour monitoring interval is far too long during the first week when electrolytes shift rapidly and can fall to dangerous levels within a day. Daily or more frequent measurement is required while the risk period lasts. (Source: RCH CPG: Eating disorders)

options.text: Continue increasing energy intake with electrolyte replacement and daily monitoring
options.rationale: Falling phosphate, magnesium and potassium in the first days of feeding is the expected biochemical signature of refeeding, caused by an insulin driven intracellular shift, and it is corrected by replacing the electrolytes rather than by withdrawing the nutrition that is treating her starvation. Australian paediatric practice has moved away from prolonged low energy protocols because underfeeding prolongs medical instability, so intake continues to advance under continuous cardiac monitoring with at least daily electrolytes and prompt replacement. (Source: RCH CPG: Eating disorders)

options.text: Maintain intake and give a fluid bolus to correct her postural blood pressure drop
options.rationale: Volume loading a severely malnourished adolescent risks precipitating cardiac failure, because the myocardium is atrophied and cannot handle a sudden preload increase, and fluid overload is a recognised component of refeeding syndrome. Her postural drop reflects starvation related cardiovascular adaptation and improves with nutrition rather than with boluses. (Source: RCH CPG: Eating disorders)

explanation.summary: Refeeding syndrome occurs when nutrition is reintroduced to a starved patient and insulin release drives phosphate, magnesium and potassium into cells alongside a shift from fat to carbohydrate metabolism, producing the falling electrolytes seen here. Thiamine is consumed rapidly in this process and must be given before or with the first feeds. The historical response was to feed very slowly, but that approach is now recognised to cause underfeeding syndrome, in which continued weight loss and persistent bradycardia prolong medical instability and lengthen admission, and Australian paediatric practice has moved towards advancing intake while replacing electrolytes aggressively. The decisive judgement in this case is that the falling electrolytes are an expected and treatable consequence of appropriate treatment rather than evidence that the treatment is wrong. Continuous cardiac monitoring, at least daily electrolytes and prompt replacement make that approach safe, and fluid boluses are avoided because the atrophied myocardium tolerates sudden preload poorly.
key_points: Insulin driven intracellular shift of phosphate, magnesium and potassium is the mechanism of refeeding syndrome.
Thiamine must be given before or alongside the first feeds because it is consumed rapidly during refeeding.
Prolonged low energy protocols cause underfeeding syndrome and prolong medical instability.
Electrolytes require at least daily measurement with prompt replacement during the first week.
Fluid boluses risk cardiac failure because the myocardium is atrophied in severe malnutrition.
explanation.pearls: Replace the electrolytes and keep feeding rather than cutting the calories when phosphate falls in the first days of refeeding, because the fall is the expected consequence of effective treatment and prolonged underfeeding causes its own syndrome of persistent bradycardia and delayed recovery.

sources.label: Australia and New Zealand Academy for Eating Disorders

subtopic_detail: continuing or withholding an effective antipsychotic when a stable woman with schizophrenia conceives
stem:
You are the psychiatrist seeing a 30 year old woman with schizophrenia who has been well for three years on olanzapine 10 mg at night. She works part time, lives with her partner and has had no admission since her diagnosis at twenty four.

She tells you she is seven weeks pregnant and that the pregnancy is wanted and planned. She has read online that antipsychotics harm babies and has already missed four doses this week because she is frightened. She has no current psychotic symptoms, her sleep is normal and her insight is good. Her two previous relapses both followed her stopping medication, and the second involved a period of significant self neglect requiring inpatient care. Her booking bloods are normal and her body mass index is 26 kg/m2.

data_table.Examination: Mental state examination shows euthymic mood, no hallucinations or delusions, no thought disorder, good insight, no extrapyramidal signs
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, electrolytes, liver function and thyroid function within normal limits, fasting glucose 4.9 mmol/L (3.0-5.4), beta human chorionic gonadotrophin consistent with seven weeks gestation

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Continue the current antipsychotic with added foetal growth surveillance
options.rationale: The risk of relapse on stopping an effective antipsychotic is high and is itself harmful in pregnancy through self neglect, poor antenatal attendance and substance use, whereas olanzapine has not been shown to be a major teratogen. Continuing the agent that has kept her well for three years is therefore the safer course, with growth scans because of the association with large for gestational age infants and early gestational diabetes screening because of the metabolic profile. (Source: Centre of Perinatal Excellence: National Perinatal Mental Health Guideline)
source_refs: Centre of Perinatal Excellence: National Perinatal Mental Health Guideline

options.text: Stop the antipsychotic for the first trimester and restart it after organogenesis
options.rationale: Withdrawal through the first trimester is intuitively appealing and is the period of highest relapse risk following cessation, and by the time symptoms return the exposure has already occurred if it was going to. This approach reliably produces relapse without avoiding meaningful risk. (Source: Centre of Perinatal Excellence: National Perinatal Mental Health Guideline)
source_refs: Centre of Perinatal Excellence: National Perinatal Mental Health Guideline

options.text: Switch her to a first generation antipsychotic with longer established safety data
options.rationale: Older agents do have a longer record of use in pregnancy, which is a genuine argument, and switching a woman who is stable risks destabilising her for a benefit that the comparative data do not support. Any switch also introduces a period of dual or inadequate cover at the least forgiving time. (Source: Centre of Perinatal Excellence: National Perinatal Mental Health Guideline)
source_refs: Centre of Perinatal Excellence: National Perinatal Mental Health Guideline

options.text: Halve the dose for the remainder of the pregnancy to reduce foetal exposure
options.rationale: Dose reduction looks like a compromise and delivers the worst of both positions, since it leaves the foetus exposed while dropping the mother below the concentration that has maintained her remission. Increased volume of distribution and hepatic metabolism in pregnancy mean doses often need to rise rather than fall. (Source: Centre of Perinatal Excellence: National Perinatal Mental Health Guideline)
source_refs: Centre of Perinatal Excellence: National Perinatal Mental Health Guideline

options.text: Replace the antipsychotic with regular psychological therapy for the pregnancy
options.rationale: Psychological therapy is a valuable adjunct in schizophrenia and improves function and adherence, and it does not substitute for antipsychotic medication in preventing relapse of a psychotic illness. Offering it as a replacement would leave her unprotected during a recognised period of vulnerability. (Source: Centre of Perinatal Excellence: National Perinatal Mental Health Guideline)
source_refs: Centre of Perinatal Excellence: National Perinatal Mental Health Guideline

explanation.summary: The instinct to stop psychotropic medication in pregnancy usually does more harm than good in established psychotic illness, because relapse carries substantial risks to both mother and foetus through self neglect, disengagement from antenatal care, substance use and, at the extreme, suicide. Olanzapine and the other second generation antipsychotics have not been shown to be major teratogens, so the balance favours continuing an agent that has maintained three years of remission. Specific monitoring is added rather than the drug being changed: growth scans because of the association with large for gestational age infants, and early screening for gestational diabetes given the metabolic profile. Abrupt cessation, dose halving and switching agents each risk destabilising a well woman without a demonstrated safety gain. She also needs a plan for the postnatal period, which carries the highest relapse risk of all.
key_points: Relapse of psychotic illness in pregnancy carries substantial risk to mother and foetus.
Second generation antipsychotics have not been shown to be major teratogens.
Switching or reducing an effective agent in pregnancy risks relapse without a demonstrated safety benefit.
Olanzapine is associated with large for gestational age infants and gestational diabetes, warranting added monitoring.
The postnatal period carries the highest relapse risk and requires a documented plan made antenatally.
explanation.pearls: Address the fear rather than the prescription when a pregnant woman with schizophrenia starts missing doses, because relapse is the largest modifiable risk to her pregnancy and stopping through the first trimester exposes the foetus during organogenesis anyway while guaranteeing she loses her remission.

sources.label: Centre of Perinatal Excellence: National Perinatal Mental Health Guideline
